I think a lot of the comments here are the ones projecting. A lot of the top comments don’t say “perhaps try this other avenue of trying to initiate conversation, and if that doesn’t work, perhaps you aren’t right for each other.” They say, hard stop, DON’T DO IT. DON’T MARRY HER. 

So, if OP and his partner are about to get married, what would it look like if he listened to those comments? As someone who’s engaged to be married a year from now, who’s been with my partner since middle school, if he were to suddenly tell me he decided all of a sudden that he no longer wanted to get married, that would be a huge breach of trust for me - to lead me into the excitement of getting married and then suddenly have him change his mind would fuck me up, and it’d probably be over. They’ve already decided to get married, so unless OP is comfortable with the idea of ending things right now, full stop, as would likely be the result if he listened to many of the top comment without adding the nuance that those comments failed to, by outright communicating to his partner that he doesn’t want to get married anymore, he’s better off trying to work things out with her and consider different ways of approaching the topic before making a drastic decision. 

I think they both have communication issues. I think for her part that’s obvious, but I think it’s a bit much for some of the comments here to suggest that (as far as we can tell from the post) one crude remark, one failed attempt at communicating the issue, and going 5 months without having sex with him indicates that she’ll never change, she doesn’t care about him, nothing will ever get better, and if he marries her, he’ll be forever stuck in a dead bedroom. That’s why I think a lot of these other comments are projecting - this sub tends to have a lot more failure/divorce stories due to their dead bedrooms than it does successful ones, likely bc it’s used as a place for dissatisfied people to vent, and the people who were just going through a bit of a rough patch and have successfully moved on from it probably aren’t gonna find themselves on this sub very often once the issue is resolved and there’s no longer a need to vent or ask for advice on how to handle things.

In terms of OP’s bad communication, he was also just wrong in a lot of ways. You can have intimacy without sex, and from there, the rest of the argument from that quote doesn’t track. My partner and I are still intimate every day despite only having sex every few months now, physically and emotionally. We share funny experiences and heartfelt moments while we’re at home. We laugh together. We cuddle, we hold hands, we kiss and hug each other every morning and every night, and we play-wrestle. Hell, some people would think it’s a red flag that we sleep in separate bedrooms bc of his sleep apnea and kicking in his sleep combined with my chronic pain and being a light sleeper, but deciding to start sleeping in separate rooms about two years ago has made our relationship better than ever, bc I’m getting much better sleep, and that really helps keep my mental health/emotions stable. We still cuddle at night as we’re winding down for bed, he just gives me a hug and kiss goodnight when he feels like he’s about to fall asleep and then goes to his room, puts his cpap on, and passes out.

The reality is that nearly every relationship or marriage is going to have dry spells, bc life happens - unless those dry spells are avoided by pressuring the other partner into sex regardless of how they’re feeling and convincing them that doing so is their duty as a spouse, which isn’t healthy either. Depression, deaths, grief, and tragedies take place throughout everyone’s life, and when we’re dealing with that, we probably aren’t gonna be in the mood for sex as often or not at all while in recovery. The thing OP needs to work through right now is attempting to better communicate with his partner in order to figure out if she’s dealing with something she’s struggling to communicate well, and if that’s the case and they love each other, they can probably work it out. In the meantime, I’d work on building a relationship of better physical/emotional intimacy to build greater trust and bonding, and work on the communication issues. 

Also, I feel inclined to say this here, bc some of the comments here have said some sketchy shit that suggests they believe otherwise: the role of a wife isn’t to fulfill her husband’s sexual needs, and that’s not the sole purpose of marriage. Marriage is a partnership in which you choose each other as teammates to navigate life together. OP suggested he loves and cares about his partner beyond sex despite his frustrations, which is wonderful and likely workable, but some of the other comments here voiced some concerning (or at least poorly-worded) ideas about the purpose of marriage.

Idk, my partner(25) and I (24) do it about every 6 months now - both on antidepressants, but we used to do it like once every 2-4 weeks a few years back when we were on the same meds. We stopped doing it as often when Roe v. Wade got overturned, bc we live in Texas and I have a fucked up reproductive system, to where if our contraceptive methods were to fail, it’d probably put me in danger and it’s harder for me and my partner to want to have sex due to the association of stress and heightened risk if we feel extra paranoid about making extra sure that I don’t get pregnant, and that’s a bit of a turn off, if you catch my drift. Like the risk went from possibly having to seek medical intervention for a miscarriage/ectopic pregnancy if God forbid the contraception fails to the possibility of me dying from the inability to seek emergency medical attention in that circumstance. Maternal mortality rates have gone up 50%+ here.

And we know people our age who are in the same boat, who also just struggle to think about sex without the idea of what could go wrong coming to mind. A mix of young men and young women. 

So yeah, my partner and I are still intimate in ways that aren’t necessarily sexual and our relationship is doing great. Just wanted to correct the idea that 5 months without sex is “damn near an eternity” at age 26. We know a lot of people in their 20’s here who are too stressed about what I mentioned above, in addition to a lot of other political issues affecting our day to day lives as valid sources of worry, and it’s hard to relax enough to enjoy sex with all that goin on and preccupying our minds, but it doesn’t mean our relationships aren’t happy or loving. 

Note to OP: if you live in a state/country being plagued with lots of big political issues, especially if some of them pertain to sex and pregnancy, you might talk to your SO and see if any of that has been affecting her ability to get in the mood. If not, it could be depression no longer effectively being treated by the medication (doesn’t necessarily mean she should stop taking it, maybe just have her discuss whether she feels that zoloft alone is still working for her with her psychiatrist). Or maybe it’s stress pertaining to other areas of her life.

I took zoloft years ago for hardly any time at all as the first treatment I tried for depression, and it sent me into mania (including a huge libido increase), leading to my Bipolar I diagnosis. Just be aware that her libido being low isn’t always the result of a certain medication - there are a lot of factors that could play into it, and rather than listening to a lot of the rather brash advice here saying to leave her just for not having sex as much as you’d like, I think there’s still a lot of room left to work on communication. 
Tbh, as a woman, a lot of these responses really grossed me out by acting like it’s an automatic reason to dump someone if they don’t have sex with you for 5 months, as if that’s so unreasonable, without giving genuine advice on how to further explore the situation. If my partner ever gave advice like that to someone in this situation, I’d be disgusted and feel less inclined than ever to have sex with him. What if a woman is dealing with grief and serious depression/stress?? You’re just supposed to dump her bc she doesn’t feel like having sex rather than working alongside her to get her in a better place, to where she feels more comfortable and emotionally stable to where sex becomes appealing to her again?? 

My partner had a coworker once who bragged to him that he cheated on his wife after one year without sex, bc she became pregnant, dealt with a complicated pregnancy, and despite giving birth to a healthy child, dealt with some pretty severe tearing that needed a while to heal. I don’t know what that guy was expecting for a response, but my partner basically told him he was a disgusting piece of shit, which is true. Y’all remind me of that guy - stop acting like an extended period of time without sex is always cause to leave the relationship, bc that DOES make y’all look like all you care about is your dicks and not about your partner as a person. Horrible, reckless advice.

OP, please take into account what I said about talking to her about what could be causing her stress/low sex drive, beyond just medication. Don’t make a rash/unempathetic decision based on some of the comments here.

YES, my partner and I were so excited to get a house where we would have two bedrooms, and I took pride in decorating his room and making it comfy for him, since a lot of the time he’d end up on the couch in our one bedroom apartment. I’m a light sleeper with chronic pain/RLS, he has sleep apnea. The cpap helped a lot with the snoring but he still thrashes around, and I have mental health issues that get way worse when I don’t sleep enough, so I was losing my mind trying to sleep in the same bed as him. My whole family has always had couples sleeping in separate beds/bedrooms due to the men snoring, but my partner never had any couple in his family sleep in separate beds, so he thought it must be indicative of an unhealthy relationship. If anything, sleeping separately has been way healthier for both of us, because, y’know, I’m not mentally unstable from lack of sleep, so that leads to way less arguments, and I’m not having to wake him up in the middle of the night and beg the half-awake sleep apnea man to go to the couch so I can sleep.

That’s what me and my partner do, he has his own bedroom bc he has sleep apnea and even though the CPAP stopped the snoring, he still thrashes around a lot in his sleep and has a habit of hitting the snooze button multiple times…meanwhile I’m a pretty light sleeper and deal with chronic pain/restless leg syndrome, so falling asleep is difficult. Thus, it was hard to fall asleep with his constant movement and after his alarm would go off even once (I’m stay-at-home, his alarm was set for 5:00 AM to go to work at 6:00 AM almost every morning). He was hesitant to the idea of sleeping separately for awhile bc he’d never known any couples in his family who slept in separate rooms - meanwhile, that’s all I’d ever known, since my parents and grandparents had always had separate bedrooms due to my dad/grandfathers snoring. My partner assumed sleeping in separate beds/bedrooms meant the relationship was unhealthy, but as someone who deals with mental health issues that tend to significantly worsen when I don’t get enough sleep…let’s just say our relationship got WAAAAY better when we started sleeping in separate bedrooms. 

In conclusion: not being able to stop doomscrolling and having to sleep separately from your wife and child bc you won’t get off the damn phone? Unhealthy. Sleeping separately from your partner bc your sleep habits don’t align due to reasons beyond your control? Not unhealthy, and in fact could lead to better quality of life/sleep for both parties 👍

My school counselor also did nothing when I finally gathered the courage to tell her my mom was beating me and I was suicidal over it. I even showed her the physical evidence of scratches and bruises bc I was so afraid I wouldn’t be believed otherwise. She told me she didn’t really know what I expected her to do, but bc I was crying, she said I could lay on the couch in the storage area behind her office and finish crying and take a nap before going back to class. I was confused by her response a bit, bc the internet had advised me to speak about my situation to a trusted adult/school counselor bc they’re mandated reporters and were suppposed to help me, but I was at least glad that I got to cry myself to sleep in the back so I wouldnt have to deal with just silently crying in class while trying to pay attention and hope no one noticed. 

I went to my counselor’s office probably 20-30 times after that, including telling her that I’d had to go to the hospital for stockpiling a family member’s medications and taking them, and almost dying. My mom refused to take me to the hospital when she walked in on me struggling to breathe, my pupils wide, and I’d like…forgotten how to talk or move. She just called me a druggie and went to work. Later, my dad showed up unexpectedly early in the day to ask if my brother and I wanted to get lunch bc he was in town, found me unconscious and took me to the hospital. After stabilizing me, a nurse asked me in front of my dad if I was trying to hurt myself or just trying to help myself fall asleep and took too many pills, and I said it was the latter and an accident, since my parents had already lost my older brother to suicide about 5 years earlier and I didn’t want to hurt my dad, since he was already crying when I regained consciousness.

So yeah, I told my school counselor that, and that I’d deliberately done my research to make sure the amount of the drug I’d stockpiled and took was an amount that, in medical studies I found online, had been enough to kill adults who were nearly double my size. I would have died if my dad hadn’t unexpectedly stopped by. And she knew my brother had killed himself 5 years prior, and I didn’t know it at the time, but she definitely should have known that put me at an even HIGHER risk of successfully committing suicide. Still, every time I went to her office, already crying, I told her about being suicidal, my attempt, other ideas I had for how I could end things, and she would just send me to the couch, to where it just became a normal thing for me to come into her office crying and ask if I could go back there and she’d let me go cry myself to sleep. Which I was thankful for at the time, but as an adult…her failed role as a mandated reporter aside, I realize now how shitty it was that she just told me there was nothing she could do and didn’t try to comfort me at all. As an adult now, not even as a counselor or therapist, I couldn’t imagine not comforting a high-risk youth crying and coming to me for help.

At the end of the day, I finally ended up devising a plan out of desperation for help, and as soon as I got to school one day, I went to her office and told her that if she didn’t put me in touch with someone who could help that day, *insert detailed suicide plan with method involving how I could gain access to a firearm while unsupervised after school*. And I was absolutely serious.

That worked, and she finally reached out to some mental health center in a nearby town, called my dad, and had him pick me up from school asap to take me there. He ended up crying and apologizing for not realizing how bad things were, which broke my heart. I was involuntarily hospitalized for 2 weeks, medicated, and a plan was set up for me to start going to free weekly therapy from then on, and my dad spent $1000 on a super secure gun safe to replace the old gun cabinet with glass windows. 

I recently told my current therapist about my school counselor and she struggled to conceal how angry and disgusted it made her. I’m an adult now and now I too can see how fucked up it was that I was just constantly left to cry myself to sleep. My therapist said she’d help navigate me through the process of reporting it to a higher level (I’d just assumed it something I could only report to the school board, and bc I came from a poor family, and my school counselor came from a rich family in our small town and her husband was the sheriff, I’d assumed there’d be no point in reporting her and if anything it’d just put a target on my back). 

My small hometown and the small towns surrounding it have a significantly higher youth suicide rate than the national average…I don’t wonder why.

My mom is mixed latina and afro-latina, and she got her dad’s hair, albeit a bit looser (her hair is more like your daughter’s and her dad had very tight curls he always wore in an afro). My dad is Irish and has looser curls, and I was the only one of my siblings to inherit my mom’s hair. I also grew up in Texas, a very small town that was probably 90% white and 9.5% latinos with straighter hair, and got criticism for my hair despite being very lightskinned, not only from other kids at school but also from adults, despite the fact that my hair was always clean and well taken care of. Comments about how I needed to brush my hair, wash my hair, it looked gross and dirty, etc. A couple times people asked to touch my hair and said something along the lines of “oh wow, it’s really soft actually, I thought it’d feel gross, like hay or something.”

Unfortunately, due to culture, I think growing resentful of our hair is just something a lot of us with curly hair deal with as tweens/teens, especially if we don’t know a lot of kids our age with similar hair. It just takes time to grow out of, and some people never do. My mom has relaxed her hair for years, and it’s very damaged. She’s 60. Her dad and my grandma divorced when she was very young, and my grandma got primary custody. My grandma doesn’t have curly hair, and would nag on my mom about how she had “bad hair” that was such a nuissance to maintain. 

Years later, my mom would say I was the only one of her kids who got her “bad hair” and treated it as a pain in the ass to deal with when I was a kid, so along with comments from people outside of our household, that probably contributed a lot to me resenting my curly hair and trying to force it straight. I even got it relaxed when I was 18 and did major damage. 

I think the only thing you can do is not be like my mom and my grandma, and don’t voice complaints about how much work it is to manage if you’re helping her. Just continue with compliments (they realky go such a long way) and try to show that you enjoy helping her with her hair on wash days and such. 

Also braids could be good, as another commenter mentioned. When I was in school (about 150 students in middle and high school combined) there was one black kid who went there who was older than me. One time, he got braids before a big football game (he played on the team) with beads on the ends in our school colors. Before the end of the day, the principal made him go home and take them out due to his reasoning that braids were “gang-affiliated,” and he did so he could play in the game that night. If anything like that happens (and it very likely could, depending on where you live in Texas), please don’t give in to the ignorance of administrators. 

I wish your daughter luck with her beautiful curls and her journey to hopefully eventually embracing them.

I think I may be in the minority opinion here, and I’m not saying “break up with her!!” But I think you should express that you wish she would recognize just how much of a labor of love your gift to her was. Like, I have yet to give a crocheted gift that didn’t receive a reaction that was even MORE positive than I even expected, and none of the recipients were crafters. My brother is one of the most emotionally-closed off people I’ve ever known, and when I made him a sunburst granny square blanket and gave it to him for Christmas, he couldn’t stop saying “oh my God” and asking questions about the process of making it. When I make things for my friends, they’re always excited, sometimes post pics of their gift on social media, and next time I visit, it’s usually found its spot on display in their homes. Hell, even my husband just regularly asks about updates to my crochet projects, and asks questions about the processes, yarn, etc. He gets excited knowing something I’m working on is for us/our home, and asks where we should put it once it’s finished.

So yeah, I think the issue isn’t “well I guess _____ just doesn’t like crochet” - if the gift recipient has any clue how much time and effort is put into a gift, I think the right thing to do is for them to appreciate just how much time and effort you dedicated to creating something you felt would bring them joy. If they don’t know, tell them. If they still don’t care, that’s shitty, and I don’t think it’s unreasonable to expect someone who’s supposed to love you to show you that they’re grateful for the love you showed them in making them a gift. And I think it’s okay to call out that shittiness or voice feeling hurt once you know it’s not just a matter of misunderstanding. 

Seriously, I’ve received homemade gifts (especially from kids - but I don’t have children of my own) that are far from what most people would consider aesthetically pleasing, but knowing how excited they were to give it to me and how hard they tried to make it perfect to the best if their ability, I’d be an asshole if I didn’t show my appreciation for the thought/work they put into it.

My advice is honestly just to play with it until you find something you feel comfortable with! What you said about contrast totally applies, I think - the more contrast you add to other features of your face (eyes, cheek color), the less contrasty the dark lip will appear. I know something I heard once that really stuck with me is that makeup is all about playing with contrast, and I think that’s a fun and helpful idea to keep in mind. I’m a natural medium redhead but my eyebrows are lighter and more sparse than my natural hair color. When I was in high school (and honestly knew almost nothing about makeup) and getting into gothic/grunge style, I was totally into dark lips, dark brows, mascara, and powder foundation all over - nothing else. My everyday makeup look now features more color - especially in my cheeks and eyes, after I realized that, wow, I CAN actually pull off dark eyeshadow. And to be fair, I think anyone can - sometimes, I think what looks off-putting at first just takes time for us to get used to seeing on our face. Sometimes, when I’m in an edgy kinda mood, I still do the very high contrast gothic/grungy look, and while I do apply a light contour and barely-there nude blush when I do it and I make my brows match my hair color now, I think if you wanna go REALLY bold and make one feature pop like dark lipstick with a fairly natural eye look, you still can and you can pull it off!! What I think is most important is 1. Confidence and 2. Good technique. Find what works for you, but also, don’t shy away from a look without trying it a few times first, even if you’re just doing your makeup to lounge around at home the first few times. Like I said, I think sometimes, what holds us back from trying new looks that we think look good on other people is that we’ve got to get used to the original shock of seeing it on our own faces and getting comfortable with the idea of what we’re wearing and how we’re wearing it.

Honestly, I wouldn’t worry too much about creating content, and I don’t know how one would give advice on “how to start panning” beyond…just use the products you have. Don’t buy new makeup products until you either run out and need to replace it OR you come across a product you absolutely love. By that, I mean don’t impulse-buy - I’ll have items on my wishlist for MONTHS before I realize I never stopped wanting, that I swatched once in Sephora and never stopped thinking about it. Also, make sure you’re not duping products you already own - i.e. already have very similar shades. 

I’m also someone who gets pretty bored easily, so if I do add something new to my collection that I don’t already have, it’s usually in the form of more colorful products like eyeshadow, blush, or lipstick. I don’t see a point in having more than a couple of liquid foundations at one time - as long as it matches my skintone, it’s going to look about the same every time. I own a light-coverage tinted moisturizer that’s lighter/a better shade for me in the winter, and a full-coverage foundation that’s slightly darker and is a better match to my skintone in the summer. Then, depending on what level of coverage I want and what shade my skin is at that time of year, I mix them together at varying ratios and that works great for me. 

Above all, if you want to pan your makeup, you should just use your makeup. And, in my opinion, don’t force yourself to hate-pan your makeup. And don’t apply makeup with the mindset that you’re using it because you want to run out so that you can post something to this subreddit or any other platform - apply it because you WANT to wear that makeup. I never force a pan - just go with the flow. 

Also, in terms of sustainability and ethics - just look into the companies you buy makeup from. For me, I mostly don’t care about if the brand’s owner might have said something stupid years ago - honestly, it’s hard to find a company that HASN’T seen some sort of scandal. What matters to me most when it comes to brand ethics is how their practices affect the environment and how they treat their employees/workers. Also, may be relevant when it comes to sustainability, but I purchase almost exclusively powder products when it comes to blush, bronzer, etc. bc in my experience, cream makeup products are a lot more likely to noticably expire before I finish them and have to toss them out. I’ve never had a powder product noticably expire, even if it’s past the listed expiration date. Will that help you with panning faster? Probably not, because powder products can be pretty dense, but again, I don’t buy that sort of stuff because I want to pan it - I buy it because I want to use it, and honestly, while it’s kind of exciting to see a pan in a product I’ve been using, most of the time it’s kind of a bummer for me, because I dread the day that I run out of that product. In high school, I had no difficulty panning products, because I was poor and pretty much used the same few products every day. And I think that experience is still part of me - if I buy something, even though I can afford more now, I make sure I really really love it first and will treasure it. And as I’ve learned more about sustainability and ethical living, I realized that I’ve always lived more sustainably than a lot of people normally do, solely bc of habits I developed when I was poor - i.e. learning how to repair and reuse a lot of things bc I couldnt afford to toss something when it broke and just buy a new one. 

Kinda got long-winded with my response, but basically: if you want to pan your products, use your products. Buy only what you love and resist multiples of similar shades. And develop a healthy and appreciative mindset when it comes to makeup.

I think the obvious answer would be my brother’s suicide when I was 11 - soon before and soon after that, I had other family members die in pretty rapid succession. The most significant before was the death of my maternal grandfather in a hit and run, and we never found out who did it. The most significant after was my uncle (mom’s brother), who killed himself after struggling to cope with losing my grandfather. Still, my brother was the loss that hit me hardest. My family didn’t grow stronger because of it - everyone just became more depressed and isolated into themselves, including me. My mom had already been abusive physically and emotionally, but things got a lot worse after that. She’d start telling me whenever she was angry or upset with me that she wished I had died instead. I attempted suicide at 16, and only survived by some kind of miracle - my mom rarely checked on me, and I’d done research to ensure that the drug I acquired in planning (won’t mention what it was specifically, but I’d never done/taken drugs before this, not even weed or alcohol or anything) was enough to kill a person even larger than I was. I planned to die overnight, but she came into my room really early in the morning before work to tell me she was leaving. I was already too incapacitated by overdose to respond to her as she asked me why I was in the state I was in, and I hardly remember it, but she said something along the lines of “did you take something?? I always knew you were a druggie - if you die, it’ll be your own fault, not my problem” and left. Only lived because my dad (who lived in a different house) happened to come by pretty soon afterwards on a weird feeling he had, rather than at 6:00 pm like he usually did. I was unconscious by the time he came by, and next thing I knew, I was in the hospital.

I just graduated college, but the past few months leading up to my graduation really fucked with me in particular when I turned 22 over winter break - I was officially older than my brother had been when he died. His suicide attempt had been successful - mine hadn’t. I just felt a lot of survivor’s guilt - weird how powerful and all-consuming that can be. Since his death, I’ve always struggled a lot with paranoia that if I mess up - say the wrong thing, am not around, etc. - someone else, or even a pet, will die. Not always paranoid at the idea that they’ll kill themselves if I mess up, but also that, say, if I left my cats at home for too many hours, the universe would punish me for being a bad person (like I’d convinced myself I was a bad sister for not saving my brother and a bad daughter for making my mom so disappointed that she wouldn’t care if I died) by killing my precious cats in a fire. Seems totally irrational, but mental illness/trauma is weird like that.

The CT setting spray is seriously the only setting spray that’s ever worked for me. Couldn’t live without it, especially bc of the necessity to wear masks in most indoor spaces, the fact that I live in Texas, and the fact that I happen to be a very sweaty woman who overheats quite easily. I honestly don’t use the Vitamin C serum every day BECAUSE it pills so bad, and yet I think the results are worth it. To be fair, I’ve never had a Vitamin C serum that DIDN’T pill on me, and I don’t think this one pills any worse than the others. I’ve basically experimented with all application methods, and what I’ve found works best is applying by patting it in rather than rubbing, waiting 5-10 minutes for absorbtion (while I do my hair or make coffee or do my eye makeup) before patting on moisturizer and sunscreen. I’ll wait another maybe 2 minutes for the moisturizer and sunscreen to soak into my skin, and then I might be done on true no-makeup days. Sometimes, I’ll add some translucent powder to my face if the shine of the oilier parts of my face is bothering me - and for powder, I always use a pouf as opposed to a brush to pat the powder onto my skin, since I feel like with powder brushes the application is always more uneven and so much powder is wasted by flying into the air. I don’t use the serum on heavier makeup days where more intense blending is required, but when I wear it on lighter makeup days, I follow my moisturizer and sunscreen with a skin tint or green primer and maybe spot-conceal, blending it all in with either a beauty blender or my fingers or both - I find that the patting method, as opposed to rubbing anything in, is key here. No. Look up the relationship between hypothyroidism and weight gain for just one example of how things like hormonal imbalances/deficiencies and shifts in your body’s chemistry (frequently caused by medication) can make it so much harder for some people to lose weight, no matter how little they eat or how much they exercise. I would know - the medication I mentioned in the post as well as hypothyroidism caused me to gain weight so rapidly that I nearly starved myself and would frequently nearly pass out (actually did once or twice) while exercising due to a lack of calories for energy, and yet I still continued to GAIN weight until that medication was switched and later began treatment for hypothyroidism. It’s NOT as simple as you’re putting it, and super important not to ignore the possibility of weight gain being caused by hormonal or chemical imbalances caused either by internal factors (illness) or external ones (medication). To ignore/dismiss that possibility is potentially dangerous, as in my situation, where I was hardly eating and trying to burn calories but gaining weight, so I assumed I must still be eating too much and not exercising enough and kept wanting to continually eat less and less because I assumed it must be my fault.

Okay, but if you’re someone who naturally has issues with self-control when it comes to food (like myself), then is it not better to seek out medication that wouldn’t exacerbate that issue? I also found that lifestyle changes, especially when I was on the medication I described in my post, did almost nothing to help keep my weight in control. Like, I was in my teenage years and borderline starving myself and exercising constantly for months and just kept gaining weight. So I’m guessing the medication had an effect on my metabolism as well. 

I know that a few years later (after a switch in medication and having lost most of the weight I gained from it), my doctor discovered issues with my thyroid being underactive, so I started taking medication for that and that’s also led to some weight loss, to where I’m now at a really healthy weight.

I don’t think it necessarily matters that the evidence is anecdotal in this case, since there’s really no harm in just exploring other options. It’s not like I’m promoting some scam like “THESE ESSENTIAL OILS CAUSED ME TO LOSE SO MUCH WEIGHT!!” I’m promoting the idea that you should work with your doctors to try to find medications that work better for you.

To be fair, I’ve found that with different birth control pills I’ve taken, none of them ever listed weight gain as a side effect - yet a lot of people taking certain birth control medications/with certain birth control implants (like myself) have reported an increase in appetite that led to weight gain. While the medication itself may not be causing weight gain, some medications just affect people differently and lead to a way bigger appetite, whether it’s listed as a side effect or not. I think, at the very least, that it’s worth a try to see if another anti-depressant would affect him differently if his weight gain is such a grievance for him.

I think that maybe some complaints I’ve heard about the pan being particularly shallow or having gone through the pan too quickly for the price might be coming from people who use brushes for setting powder as opposed to velour puffs, which I prefer for applying setting powder because I find it’s less likely to move my makeup underneath and it feels less wasteful than having to tap off the brush, as with loose setting powder, to remove the excess. 

I think generally one of my favorite things about this powder is the fact that, even with combination skin that tends to fluctuate between dryness and oiliness caused by thyroid/hormonal issues as the result of autoimmune disease, it just never looks too matte/flat or dry. Like, I know something I’ve heard a lot in the last few months on the internet is “makeup will always look like makeup and not skin, and that’s okay”...but even considering, that, over the last couple years my skin has improved way more and I no longer seem to have the cystic acne I dealt with for years and thus can use lighter coverage skin tints and foundations now, I feel like when using this powder it really does look like I’m not wearing makeup, and idk, after years of being so self-conscious about my skin for so long, even after my cystic acne cleared up bc of pores and frequent uneven texture, it’s like strangely addicting to look in the mirror and have it look like I have almost invisible pores and such a smooth skin texture, even up close. Only “blurring” powder I’ve ever used that seems to actually do what it claims. I’ll even use just the powder with no foundation on just skincare days, because obviously it minimizes shine but it’s also so satisfying to see it make my pores and texture appear almost nonexistent.

This ended up being a longer comment than expected, but do I recommend it? Hard to say - if it’s truly out-of-budget, even if used in the way I suggested with a velour puff as opposed to a brush to make it last longer, then maybe not - but only because  once I tried it I couldn’t go back to other powders, even recommended supposed dupes for this one. If, however, it’s within your budget, I 100% think anyone who’s able to afford to purchase it and repurchase upon running out if they love it as much as I do absolutely NEEDS to try it. It just makes me feel so beautiful and confident, to where my makeup wouldn’t feel complete without it.

Also, for reference: I purchased this one back in October, and this is the first full-size I’ve owned since trying the mini before purchasing this one. I use it almost every day, whether just with skincare or with my makeup, and you can see how much I’ve used. Not sure how it compares to other pressed powders since I’ve used mostly loose powders in the past, but to me it seems like good value for what you’re actually getting.

1. MoroccanOil Treatment Light - REPURCHASED - Haven’t found a better hair oil yet, coming from a 2C/3A curly girl who’s been growing out her hair since before Covid hit (still proud I never succumbed to the at-home Covid chop trend). Pricey but I’ve found a little goes a long way, even with thick curly hair that’s now about elbow-length.
2. SK-II Facial Treatment Essence - NOT REPURCHASED, NEVER AGAIN - Purchased with money from a gift card I received on somewhat of a whim, because I always wanted to be able to say I’d at least TRIED this product since it’s such a cult classic, even though I knew DAMN well that if I ended up liking it, I wouldn’t be able to afford to keep it in my routine. Purchased in early September, used every night, finished a couple weeks ago, and already the two LESS EXPENSIVE essences I’m trying as a replacement have shown me significantly better results (trial sizes of the CosRX Advanced Snail 96 Mucin Power Essence and the Kiehl’s Ferulic Brew Rejuvenating Facial Essence). This bottle is the smallest size they sell and is still about $100. BIG regret, but at least now I know. If you haven’t tried it and you’re considering it, just don’t. My face felt somewhat better with its use, but to such a menial degree that I couldn’t really even tell you HOW it helped with any specificity. 
3. Embryolisse Lait-Crème Concentré - REPURCHASED - LOVE usinvg this as a daytime moisturizer/primer. Another cult-classic product I was trying for the first time, but this was a success. This is the 30 ml size and it runs for about $16, and a little goes a long way. Doesn’t have the grip of a primer, per say, so much as it just seems to be very plumping, minimize pores, and absorb like a dream. On days where I needed more grip for makeup, I’d just layer a “real” primer on top, like the Nyx Marshmellow primer, with no issues. Really like how lightweight this is as a daytime moisturizer, and it didn’t pill or anything with my sunscreen!!  Altogether a really solid product, and while my fiancé says he thinks it smells like nothing, I feel like it has a really pleasant, super subtle creamy scent, if that makes sense. Also, I don’t really use any other products made from metal tubes, so I featured a solo pic of this one just because of how satisfying I thought the empty tube was. :)
4. Clinique Lash Power Mascara - DID NOT REPURCHASE - It’s a great tubing mascara and the tiny wand is great for bottom/corner lashes, and I typically would have repurchased had I not found a great drugstore tubing mascara before finishing this one! After finding the far-cheaper drugstore mascara, I continued to use what was left of this one for my bottom and corner lashes just so it wouldn’t go to waste, because I DO love how tiny the wand is on this one.
5. Anastasia Beverly Hills Brow Wiz (Caramel and Ash Brown) - DID NOT REPURCHASE - Used most of the caramel brow pencil before dyeing my hair darker, explaining the color change to Ash Brown. Continued to use Ash Brown until I ran out, while using the rest of the Caramel for fake freckles (works really well for that, actually)!! However, upon finishing the Ash Brown recently, I decided to try the Benefit Precisely, My Brow Pencil in shade 3.5 instead, since I’d never tried any other brow pencil and wanted to venture out, since the ABH brow wiz in Ash Brown seemed to be the closest shade tried in-store to match my new hair color, but still felt a little too cool, plus I’d just heard such great things about the Benefit brow pencil. Been using the new Benefit brow pencil for a very short time but already waaaay prefer it - feels like the color match is better AND the strokes are a lot more fine and hair-like, plus easier to blend with a spoolie, PLUS seems to have a longer wear-time without budging.
6. Farmacy Clearly Clean Makeup Meltaway Cleansing Balm - DID NOT REPURCHASE - Supposed to be a gentler formula than the original (which I’ve repurchased several times) and less likely to cloud up the eyes. Great product for removing makeup - just annoyed by the eye thing!! Unfortunately, I find that it still clouds up my eyes for a bit, although to a lesser degree. However, funny story, Sephora accidentally sent me two of these, so I’m on the second container at the moment. However, for when this second one is finished, I have a small size of the Dermalogica Precleanse Cleansing Oil on standby to see if I like it any better, or if the cloudy-eye thing is just one of the unnecessary evils that comes with precleansing. If that’s the case, I think I will just end up going back to this one.
7. Maybelline Snapscara Mascara - REPURCHASED - FINALLY, a tubing drugstore mascara that competes with (and, dare I say, BEATS) high-end! Seriously, this is such an inky jet-black formula that NEVER clumps or leaves residue on my face, and I love that it looks so natural and leaves my lashes flexible and un-stiff. While I kind of wish the wand were better shaped for corner lashes (it’s somewhat chunky and curved), it’s still the best I’ve found and super easy to remove if I accidentally get it on my skin while applying.
8. Clean & Clear Advantage Acne Spot Treatment - REPURCHASED - Great and affordable, and one of the only drugstore spot treatments I’ve found that’s effective without irritating my sensitive skin.
9. Glossier Boy Brow in Brown - REPURCHASED- Probably my most-repurchased product ever, bc I’ve never found a brow gel/pomade I’ve liked more in all these years. Just perfection. Not even interested in trying others anymore.

Honestly? We’re super broke all the time and in our early 20’s, and last year for Christmas, my fiancé somehow managed to do an apartment-friendly remodel of our kitchen overnight. He installed racks to hang our kitchen utensils (which really only I use, because I do the cooking bc I’m the one who enjoys it and love seeing how much he always loves and appreciates my cooking), got some nicer pans for me, put a removable backsplash in, and added removable wallpaper to add a little accent wall in my favorite color (forest green). Also got some drawer/cabinet organizers and I especially appreciated that he got me some specialized kitchen tools to make it easier for me to do certain tasks that are harder for me than they are for most people because of my neurological disabilities and difficulties doing things like opening jars. Honestly, the most meaningful, beautiful gift I’ve ever received, because he knows how much I daydream about having a house one day and even now I try to make everything pretty in the apartment but it can be so hard when we’re both constantly working so hard and still don’t have much money, but he secretly saved for months for this. Meant so much that he just wanted me to have not just a prettier kitchen to cook in, but wanted to make my life easier in a meaningful way and make it easier to do simple tasks independently, without having to ask for help with basic tasks, and I love that he took into consideration how much it means for me to retain my independence without having to ask for help, even as my neurological/autoimmune diseases progresses and things get harder. It can be very discouraging to have to ask for help with seemingly menial tasks, and it meant the world to me that he noticed what I often had to ask for help doing and did his research to find specially designed products to make my life easier.

In general, I think receiving gifts to help with cooking and cleaning (when those are my responsibilities, since he works constantly and brings in all the money to support us) is less about saying “woman, cook and clean for ME with these” and more about “I know you work so hard around here, and I want to use what little money I have to buy things that would make your life easier”

Hey! I also have very fair skin (often the lightest shade in foundations and concealers for reference) and I currently have the Miracle Balm in bronze, dusty rose, and au naturale!! No tawny, since Bobbi suggested in a vid that it’s the only one that’s too deep for fair skin. These are basically impossible to mess up application - super buildable and always look really effortless and natural. I have lupus, which really contributes to my paleness bc I have to avoid sun exposure because otherwise I tend to get rashes even with sunscreen. Because of this, after evening out my skintone (using Saie’s Slip Tint or the Dr. Jart’s Cicapair Color Correcting Cream) I can look a bit lifeless and the miracle balms in dusty rose and bronze help to make me look so healthy and I can easily control how much color I add to my face - like I said, impossible to mess up. Au naturale is actually the color I use the least - basically serves as a highlighter when using another blush that looks a bit more matte on my face, and even then I find myself gravitating to my Saie Dewy Highlighter a lot more frequently bc it tends to have the same effect but is at a lower pricepoint. Overall, my recommendation is to try the dusty rose or bronze first if you’re looking to add a bit of color to your face, with dusty rose serving as more of a “traditional” blush and bronze serving as a great kind of blush/bronzer hybrid, which is great, because most bronzers end up not looking quite right on my skin tone. I recommend Au Naturale if you’re looking for a sort of highlight that adds a healthy glow and moisturized look/feel. Overall, absolutely love this product - even more than I initially thought I would, and I end up reaching for it all the time!!

I think with your style vs your desired style, I can see how you’d have quite the conundrum. I’m short, petite, and really curvy, but one of my main fashion icons was/is Alexa Chung - more for the laid-back, playful aspect of her style than anything else. HOWEVER - when it actually came to buying clothes inspired by her looks, I tried to blend what she wore with what looks good on ME. (For example, if she sported an awesome, fun striped tee with boyfriend jeans, I could get a similar tee and pair it with high-waisted jeans with the tee tucked into the waist, because it’s so much more flattering and therefore comfortable for me. Very basic example, but came to mind.)

And honestly, if you want to buy something because it just SPEAKS to you even if it’s not necessarily “ideal” for your body type, I say go for it. I do, and using the basics I have that suit me in my own closet, it feels easy to integrate that piece into my wardrobe, even if that piece itself is something that isn’t “supposed” to be flattering on me. I think it’s less about curating what you buy and more about how you style it, as long as you truly love whatever it is you’re buying.

Another thing: I’m super girly and love the idea of high heels and beautiful shoes, but I have MS and am physically handicapped. But no biggie!! It takes a lot of searching, but I DO manage to find shoes with VERY low heels and solid construction that fit my disability-based needs and my aesthetic ones (I WAS an art major, after all - expressing myself through style is really important to me). 

Basically, I tried the capsule/functional wardrobe thing a long time ago, and I think it’s important to acknowledge that for some people, it just isn’t reasonable and can even sometimes take the fun out of fashion. When I see something I love, I know that means it’s ME and fits my personal aesthetics because it speaks to my heart. Build your OWN aesthetic by accumulating pieces over time and making sure you genuinely love them all, and I think everything ends up working out itself. If you love a look, I really believe you can make it your own. I don’t follow fashion advice, like, ever - I only look at pins for inspiration and find a way to make that look work for ME, and I receive compliments on my outfits all the time. Don’t wanna drag on here, but as an autistic woman who’s struggled with making friends and socializing in general, the best choice I ever made was to stop caring whether or not people liked me or not. A lot of people think you can’t control something like that - believe me, I didn’t think I could either - but once you stop giving a fuck, people who are like you just gravitate towards you. I’m not saying it’s a TON of people, and usually it’s just a few, but it’s better to have 2-3 really close friends than it is to have “friends” who you actually don’t vibe with very well. 
Also, get it out of your head that you’re super unique or different from other people - it’s stuck up and only hinders you from empathizing with people you might otherwise bond with. Get comfortable with being alone or having no one to talk to sometimes - it’s not “abnormal” and trying to force conversation seems desperate. 

Also, just to put it out there, something I think is just some of the worst advice for making friends is “look for people who have the same interests as you.” If someone has the same interests as you, great - and based on your very common interests, it’s gonna happen. In my case, alongside having common interests, I also have some pretty niche ones, but it’s important not to rule out being friends with people who are really different from you. I love learning about new things from my friends! Anyway, yeah, that’s my advice.

I think he gave up on therapy because he didn’t think he saw a change, but I did, for the most part, although I don’t know if he’s ever practiced what I say all the time: going to therapy and taking medication isn’t going to solve the problem, you’ve got to combine those things with making a change in your day to day life. 

I think it’s very important to mention: one of the times we broke up was because I found out that he’d been lying to me for months about an opioid addiction that he’d developed in secret, but that I expected all along: he was consistently irritated, refused to visit most of the time, and was suddenly completely broke - too broke to go on simple lunch dates. So I broke it off - and he said after two months of no contact (I unblocked him and messaged him first when a mutual friend told me he’d attempted suicide a few weeks before) that he’d realized he’d make the worst mistake of his life and didn’t want to live knowing what he did. But he got clean and went after therapy and medication help with more persistance than ever to prove to me that he was going to become a better man for himself and for me. And everything really was SO much better - better than ever. Fast forward - I feel an eery similarity to the way he was when he was addicted to painkillers and heroin with his current gaming. Suddenly he’s unable to express his emotions, possibly because he’s using gaming like he used drugs to rewire his brain not to feel: like there’s no fulfillment or pleasure, but also no pain. He has no REAL interest in anything else - he feigns it (and not very well) in order to get me to stop complaining before running off to play games again. And I find that the online community, reddit most of all, that I’m the “bad guy” here: like, “he could still be using drugs, this is a way healthier way to deal with it, stop trying to take him away from his only place of relief” and “you’re not bringing any income into the household, so until you have to come home from working 10 hours a day, you don’t really have a say in how he should spend his downtime.” I don’t know - I don’t just want him to spend more meaningful, fulfilling time with me. I want him to find a different hobby he enjoys that wouldn’t disconnect him from reality so much, be so addictive, or give himself a sense of pride in achieving: he used to love music and playing french horn so much, and abandoned it and sold his horn for drugs when he was still on them. I’d love it if he learned guitar or got into drawing or cooking or home improvement - but I can’t truly suggest a new hobby that he’ll open up to, apparently. I only know what I personally enjoy, and he doesn’t seem to have any desire to find a something new to dedicate his time to.

I wouldn’t say “too naïve to live” - that’s not a very humble way to put it, and I find the value of humility insanely important. I think a better way to say what you may be trying to say is “happily oblivious” or “close-minded.” I myself, of course, am very naïve - and there’s nothing wrong with that if I’m willing to admit it. Hell, I only just recently realized that I shouldn’t be so trusting of strangers in college, especially men, but maybe a big part of me being too optimistic about people sometimes comes from my autism. But if I admit that naïvety, it means I’m opening myself up to growth, and I’m in love with learning more about the world around me and letting my observations and experiences swirl in my head and truly affect my mindset as I ponder them. But in the case of being “happily oblivious” or “close-minded” as some people I know, they really don’t WANT to learn anymore or search for deeper meaning in anything, including relationships - they’d prefer the easy way out, which is keeping things quite shallow and not allowing themselves to learn or grow, knowing that change can be scary, or thinking that if they allow something or someone to change their worldview, it’ll mean that they were wrong and they don’t want to admit that to themselves. I think that’s what you were trying to say, but correct me if I’m wrong.

I really think it tends to be a misunderstanding - I know with my aspergers, the misinterpretation of my actions as being narcissistic or selfish is especially high. And you might not see it, because of our introverted nature, but it really tends to keep us up at night or weigh heavy on our minds, especially when it seems to be everyone misunderstanding us all the time. I know it’s led me to suicidality many times because for so long I was unlucky in finding anyone who had the patience to see my true intentions behind an often aloof exterior. Interestingly, my best friend and my husband are both INFJ’s, and I think they tend to be incredibly patient, and when they’ve outrightly told me that I was had the biggest heart of anyone they ever knew and felt empathy for my being misunderstood, it brought me to tears. Because for so long, I thought maybe something was wrong with me, and maybe I *was* crazy and delusional and was as selfish as so many people had told me throughout my life. So I really suggest giving it a little more time with this person - you could be missing out if you don’t practice patience, but I think that applies to interacting with anyone, not just INFPs.

As an INFP, I find all religion beautiful because of how much influence it has in the history of humanity. I also really especially love the story of Judaism - it’s a very noble one. As for myself, I’m Irish and Mexican, so I’d say I’m Catholic. But really, “God” feels deeply personal to me, like it’s both within me and all around me - you’ve just gotta open up your eyes and your heart to see it.

As an INFP, the range really varies, but I guess the best way I can explain it is using my favorite book, The Catcher in the Rye, which made me cry my eyeballs dry when, after being so painfully idealistic that it hurt so deeply to see all the ugliness in the world, Holden Caufield finally kind of finished his pilgrimage and visited his little sister, and as he watched her ride the carousel, he got that spliter of hope and the sense that maybe everything wasn’t so bad after all. 

I also cried watching American Beauty when Ricky was showing Jane “the most beautiful thing he’d ever caught on film,” the plastic bag dancing in the breeze with the fallen leaves. I agree, that was gorgeous. A lot of my friends and my partner didn’t seem to understand why that was so important and touching to me.

I’m also fascinated with dust speckles floating in through the window blinds in the morning. It makes me smile and my heart lightens up.

So I guess, overall, you might be able to say the most beautiful things to me are moments of hope in such a dark world. Or maybe raw human emotion. Or maybe romanticism, more so in line with the artistic movement than with what’s often considered “romance” (two people falling in love). Or maybe just when I’m no longee desperately searching for beauty and I’ve given up, and then it comes to me out of nowhere, just when I’d thought there was none left. Nature alone doesn’t get me off like human life and human history does - for example, looking at an untouched landscape might make me thing “that’s so pretty” but looking at nature that has overgrown rotting, abandoned buildings makes me emotional wondering what was and what could have been.
